Memorial Ship Mikasa

Location82-19 Inaokacho, Yokosuka, Kanagawa 238-0003, Japan
Visited15 May 2005, 27 Oct 2013
WebsiteMemorial Ship Mikasa

Museum Report

Battleship Mikasa was built by Vickers in England, and commissioned in 1902 – last of the six British-built first class battleships operated by the Imperial Japanese Navy at the start of the 1904-05 Russo-Japanese war. She served as the flagship of Admiral Togo, including at the Battle of Tsushima. On the night of 11/12 September 1905 – six days after the Treaty of Portsmouth ended the Russo-Japanese war, Mikasa suffered an accidental explosion and sank in the port of Sasebo, however she was refloated in August 1906 and returned to service in August 1908. She operated through World War One and in the Vladivostok area during the Russian Revolution.

Mikasa was nominated to be disposed of in the 1922 Washington Naval Treaty. In 1923, with Mikasa lying idle in anticipation of her scrapping, the Japan Times launched a media campaign to save her, and by March 1924 Japanese associations were presenting petitions to the embassies of the WNT signatories seeking permission to retain Mikasa as a museum. In November/December 1924, France, Italy, Great Britain and the US all advised Japan that they had no objection to the preservation of Mikasa in perpetuity as a national memorial. In 1926 Mikasa was commemorated as a memorial and transferred to the Mikasa Preservation Society.

In 1945 Mikasa again faced an uncertain future. By the direction of the Allied Occupation Forces stationed in Japan, the bridges, masts, guns, funnels and other structures were removed, leaving a hulk that was used for a while as a ‘night club’. In the late 1950’s a campaign to restore Mikasa, with support from Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz resulted in Mikasa being restored as a museum ship.

Memorial Ship Mikasa is encased in concrete in Yokohama. You have full access to the upper deck and 1 deck. Given the devastation brought about by her dual demilitarisations, much of the structure, equipment and ship fittings are replicas, however it has been very well done. There is no machinery left on the ship, however below deck there is a large gallery on the Russo-Japanese war, and the Battle of Tsushima – including a large mechanical model which re-enacts the movement of the two fleets during the battle. Signage on the ship is bi-lingual.

Getting to Mikasa by public transport from Tokyo is easy – it is a short walk from Yokosuka-Chuo train station. Note that this is different to Yokosuka station, which is on a different line – if you go to the wrong station, you will have to either catch a bus, or take a quite lengthy walk to get to Mikasa.

There was no shop when I visited Mikasa, however they did sell a very good guide book in English.

It is hard to over-state the importance of Mikasa. As the only surviving battleship of her generation, the only remaining British-built battleship, and the only surviving significant warship that served in the Imperial Japanese Navy, she is unique in many ways. She belongs in the bucket-list of anyone interested in early 20th century naval history.
